passage:
At nine, Divyansh slid a maths test with a red 8 under his pillow. His father Vijay had a single question at dinner: "What was your score?" When it wasn't full marks, he said nothing and went out to the balcony. Divyansh concluded that good marks meant love, and that mistakes were best kept out of sight.

At twenty-one, Divyansh sat in front of an internship form with the closing date on Friday. The résumé needed one more line, the cover letter one more polish, and the photo was slightly off. He told himself he would submit tomorrow when everything was ready. Friday came and went. So did the next form. His friend Bhavna asked, "Did you send it?" and Divyansh said, "Almost." He felt relief and dread at the same time. Doing nothing felt safer than sending something imperfect, and yet it meant the one outcome he feared.

That weekend, Bhavna sat beside him. "Send it rough," she said. "I'll sit right here." He winced, but he sent the next application at eleven at night.

qa.q: What did Vijay ask Divyansh at dinner?
How does the atmosphere at home when Divyansh is nine connect to his missed deadlines at twenty-one?
qa.a: At nine Divyansh learns from Vijay that marks bring warmth and mistakes are best hidden, and at twenty-one the same fear keeps him polishing forms until the deadlines pass, because doing nothing feels safer than sending anything imperfect.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he told Bhavna the form was almost sent?
qa.a: Divyansh felt relief and dread at once, afraid of sending something imperfect but also aware that the deadline had passed.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that helped Divyansh act?
qa.a: Bhavna encouraged him to send it rough and offered to sit with him, which made the risk of an imperfect application easier to take.

grounding: Perfectionism linked across ages: a child learning that love follows marks, and the young adult who lets deadlines pass because nothing feels ready.
